name: champion’s portion

attributes.attribute: best share of the meat at the feast
won the right to carve the great pig
proved itself champion in the feast of Briciu
sets the scene in Gaul for the great meats
Old Irish form curadmir, Modern Irish curadhmír
also known as the hero's portion
share of beef or pork given to the hero of the hour

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Champion’s portion names the choice share of meat at a Celtic feast. MacKillop traces the term to Old Irish curadmir and gives Modern Irish curadhmír. The strongest warrior received the curad-mir, the best cut of the beef or pork, often read as the thigh. When two warriors claimed it, they fought at once. The duel could continue to the death. MacKillop calls the winner the hero of the hour and records hero's portion as another name for the custom. Records place the custom around the first century BCE. Two great Irish tales turn on this rule. In the feast of Bricriu, the champion's portion drives the hero to prove himself the boldest. In the story of Mac's pig, Conall Cernach earns the right to carve the great boar. The Greek writer Posidonius set the same scene in Gaul. He reported two warriors dueling for the prized cut. Athenaeus carried his account onward. MacKillop cites Posidonius as proof of the custom's great age. Homer gave Ajax a like honour after victory. Welsh tradition keeps the theme softly. It grants the chief man the best seat and the finest cup.

okr.objective: The champion's portion gave the top warrior the best meat and forced rivals to duel for it.
key_results: MacKillop derives the custom from Old Irish curadmir.
The winner of the duel earns the name hero of the hour.
Posidonius of the first century BCE confirms the custom's antiquity.
The tales of Bricriu's feast and Mac Da Tho's pig both turn on this rule.
